abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Mosunetuzumab is approved as an intravenous (IV) formulation for relapsed/refractory (R/R) follicular lymphoma (FL) after ≥ 2 prior therapies. A subcutaneous (SC) formulation, aiming to improve patient safety and convenience, has been developed. We report the primary analysis of pharmacokinetics (PK), efficacy, and safety of mosunetuzumab SC (N = 94; median follow‐up: 26.1 months) at the recommended Phase 2 dose (Cycle [C]1 Day [D]1: 5 mg; C1D8 and D15, and C2D1 onwards: 45 mg) in patients with R/R FL after ≥ 2 prior therapies, alongside data from a within‐study comparator cohort of mosunetuzumab IV in a similar patient population (N = 90; median follow‐up: 22.5 months). The co‐primary PK endpoints (Ctrough and AUC) were met, demonstrating non‐inferior exposure of mosunetuzumab SC versus IV (observed Ctrough[C3]: geometric mean ratio [GMR] 1.39 [90% confidence interval (CI): 1.20–1.61]; AUC0–84: GMR 1.06 [90% CI: 0.92–1.21]). Mosunetuzumab SC efficacy was consistent with IV: overall response rate, 76.6% (95% CI: 66.7–84.7); complete response rate, 61.7% (95% CI: 51.1–71.5); median duration of complete response, 34.6 months (95% CI: 20.7–not evaluable [NE]); and median progression‐free survival, 23.7 months (95% CI: 14.6–NE). Mosunetuzumab SC demonstrated a favorable safety profile versus mosunetuzumab IV with a numerically lower rate (29.8% vs. 44.4%) and severity (grade ≥ 2: 9.6% vs. 18.9%) of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) events. Mosunetuzumab SC combines the benefits of short administration time, fixed‐duration treatment, outpatient accessibility, and low CRS rate, offering clinically meaningful improvements in patient convenience and safety.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Many patients with follicular lymphoma (FL) experience disease relapse after initial therapy, with decreasing progression‐free survival (PFS) after multiple lines of treatment [1, 2, 3]; therefore, effective novel therapies are needed to improve survival outcomes for patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) FL. T‐cell therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cell therapies and bispecific antibodies, have transformed the treatment landscape for R/R FL, offering clinical benefit to patients in whom multiple lines of therapy have failed [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9].

Mosunetuzumab, a CD20 × CD3 T‐cell engaging bispecific antibody, targets and eliminates normal and malignant B cells [10, 11]. The intravenous (IV) formulation of mosunetuzumab, administered with no hospitalization requirement, received accelerated approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and was granted conditional marketing authorization by the European Medicines Agency as the first bispecific antibody for the treatment of patients with R/R FL who have received ≥ 2 prior systemic therapies [12, 13]. In a pivotal Phase 2 study of 90 patients with R/R FL [9, 14, 15], mosunetuzumab IV demonstrated an objective response rate (ORR) of 80% with 60% of patients having complete responses (CR) and median PFS of 17.9 months, with consistent efficacy in patients with high‐risk disease features and a manageable safety profile [9]. Thirty‐five (64.8%) patients with a CR remained in remission after 4 years or more of follow‐up [15].

Subcutaneous (SC) treatment administration has the advantage of reducing treatment time and improving convenience for patients and healthcare systems, compared with IV infusion. SC administration delays and reduces peak drug concentrations, which can theoretically lead to improved safety versus IV administration due to a reduction in the rate of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) events associated with T‐cell engaging bispecific antibodies [16]. T‐cell engaging bispecific antibodies approved for the treatment of R/R FL are administered either IV or SC [16], and there are limited head‐to‐head data available to compare the safety and efficacy of these modes of administration [17]. A SC formulation of mosunetuzumab has been developed and, in the dose escalation portion of the Phase 1/2 study that established the recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D), mosunetuzumab SC demonstrated promising efficacy with a manageable safety profile in patients with R/R B‐cell non‐Hodgkin lymphoma [18, 19].

We present pharmacokinetic (PK), efficacy, safety, health‐related quality of life (HRQoL), and exploratory pharmacodynamic data from the primary analysis of mosunetuzumab SC at the RP2D [19] in a pivotal Phase 2 dose expansion cohort of patients with R/R FL after ≥ 2 prior therapies. Data are reported alongside results from a within‐study Phase 2 expansion comparator cohort of mosunetuzumab IV in a similar patient population.

sec.title: Study Design and Participants
sec.p: This was a Phase 1/2, multicenter, open‐label study (NCT02500407) of mosunetuzumab in patients with R/R B‐cell hematologic malignancies. We report data from a pivotal Phase 2 dose expansion cohort for patients with R/R FL treated with mosunetuzumab SC. Data from the pivotal cohort for mosunetuzumab IV are presented as a within‐study comparator [9] with a clinical cutoff date of January 3, 2022, selected to provide a similar follow‐up to the SC cohort. The clinical cutoff date for the PK analyses in the IV cohort was August 27, 2021.

Eligible patients were aged ≥ 18 years, had histologically confirmed FL (grade 1–3a), an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1, and had previously received ≥ 2 lines of systemic therapy including anti‐CD20 therapy and an alkylating agent. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are listed in the Supplementary Methods.

This study was conducted in full conformance with the International Council for Harmonisation E6 guideline for Good Clinical Practice and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, or the applicable laws and regulations of the country in which the research was conducted, whichever afforded greater protection to the individual. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Study Treatment
sec.p: Mosunetuzumab SC was administered in 21‐day cycles at the previously identified RP2D with step‐up dosing in Cycle (C)1 (C1 Day [D]1: 5 mg; C1D8, C1D15, C2D1 and onwards: 45 mg). Mosunetuzumab SC injections were administered over approximately 30–60 s. At the onset and towards the end of the study, a single dose of 20 mg dexamethasone or 80 mg methylprednisolone was given (orally or IV) before each mosunetuzumab administration. For part of the study, 10 mg dexamethasone was administered orally before mosunetuzumab administration and again on the next 2 consecutive days. Hospitalization was not mandatory for mosunetuzumab SC administration. Patients who achieved CR by C8 completed treatment; those with a partial response or stable disease at C8 could continue treatment for up to a total of 17 cycles at the physician's discretion.

sec.title: Study Outcomes
sec.p: The co‐primary PK endpoints to demonstrate PK non‐inferiority (PKNI) of mosunetuzumab SC compared with mosunetuzumab IV were: observed C3 (i.e., pre‐C4 dose) serum Ctrough concentration (Ctrough[C3]) and predicted cumulative area under the concentration‐time curve over 0–84 days (AUC0–84). PKNI was defined as having lower bounds of the 90% confidence intervals (CI) of the geometric mean ratio (GMR) for the observed Ctrough(C3) and predicted cumulative AUC0–84 above the predefined threshold of 0.8. Full details of the PK statistical methods and the PKNI patient population (with exclusions) are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Secondary efficacy endpoints included CR rate and ORR (both as best response), duration of response (DOR), duration of CR (DOCR), and PFS (all by investigator and independent review committee assessment using International Harmonization Project response criteria [20]), and overall survival (OS). Full definitions of secondary efficacy endpoints are listed in the Supplementary Methods. Exploratory subgroup analyses of response rates and time‐to‐event endpoints in patients with high‐risk disease characteristics were also performed. A prespecified sensitivity analysis excluded patients who died or discontinued treatment due to COVID‐19 prior to having any tumor assessments (Supplementary Methods).

Tumor assessments by computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans were performed at screening, 6 weeks (optional), 3 months, and once every 3 months thereafter during study treatment. Following completion of therapy, tumor assessment by CT with or without PET scans was performed every 3 months during the first 18 months after study enrollment, at 24 months (from C1D1), and once every 12 months thereafter. A bone marrow examination was performed at baseline; if bone marrow involvement was observed, a bone marrow examination was required for confirmation of CR (within 42 days of radiographic CR).

Safety and tolerability were assessed by incidence, nature, and severity of adverse events (AEs), and by changes in laboratory parameters. AEs were graded using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 4.0) and assessed using preferred terms (specific terms) and high‐level terms (grouped terms) as defined by MedDRA (version 26.1). CRS was graded using the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy criteria [21]. Exploratory pharmacodynamic analyses were performed and are detailed in the Supplementary Methods.

HRQoL was assessed using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire‐Core 30 (EORTC QLQ‐C30) for physical functioning and fatigue, and the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy‐Lymphoma subscale (FACT‐LymS) for lymphoma symptoms [22, 23]. Further details are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Simulations with the current population PK SC/IV model projected GMRs of 1.06 and 1.57 for the co‐primary endpoints of AUC0–84 and Ctrough(C3). Based on these GMRs and a 50% co‐efficient of variance, approximately 36 patients were needed to establish the PKNI with 80% power and one‐sided alpha of 0.05; therefore, the sample size of 94 patients provided sufficient power for the PKNI analyses. The PKNI population included per‐protocol PK‐evaluable patients who received the drug material created using an updated drug substance process and had at least one post‐baseline measurable PK concentration.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographics and baseline characteristics. For ORR and CR, exact 95% CIs were calculated using the Clopper–Pearson method. Kaplan–Meier estimates were provided for DOCR, DOR, PFS, and OS. Brookmeyer–Crowley methodology was used to construct 95% CIs for the median DOCR, DOR, PFS, and OS; Greenwood's formula was used to construct 95% CIs for landmark analyses.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Between April 2021 and February 2023, 94 patients with R/R FL were enrolled and received mosunetuzumab SC at the RP2D [19] (intent‐to‐treat population). At clinical cutoff (July 24, 2024), 60 patients (63.8%) had completed initial treatment and 34 patients (36.2%) had discontinued treatment (Figure S1). Reasons for treatment discontinuation were death (n = 4), disease progression (n = 22), AEs (n = 4), physician decision (n = 1), withdrawal (n = 2), and loss to follow‐up (n = 1). Median time (range) on study was 26.1 (1–40) months.

For the within‐study mosunetuzumab IV comparator cohort, 90 patients with R/R FL were enrolled between May 2019 and September 2020 and received mosunetuzumab IV with step‐up dosing in C1 (C1D1: 1 mg; C1D8: 2 mg; C1D15: 60 mg; C2D1: 60 mg; C3D1 and onwards: 30 mg) [9]. At clinical cutoff, median time (range) on study was 22.5 (2–32) months. The median (range) number of treatment cycles received in both the mosunetuzumab SC and IV cohorts was 8 (1–17).

In the mosunetuzumab SC cohort, median age (range) was 65 (35–84) years, 41 patients (43.6%) were female, 82 patients (87.2%) had Ann Arbor stage III/IV disease, and the median (range) number of prior lines of therapy received was 3 (2–8). Fifty‐nine patients (62.8%) were refractory to their last prior therapy, and 44 patients (46.8%) were double refractory to prior anti‐CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy and an alkylating agent. Progression of disease within 24 months from the start of first line therapy had occurred in 41 patients (43.6%). Baseline characteristics were generally balanced with the mosunetuzumab IV cohort (Table 1).

sec.title: PK Non‐Inferiority Analysis
sec.p: In the mosunetuzumab SC cohort, 68/94 patients were included in the PKNI‐evaluable population (clinical cutoff for PK analysis: February 1, 2024; patients who received study treatment prior to an updated drug substance process were excluded, see Supplementary Methods); 90/90 patients in the mosunetuzumab IV cohort were included. PKNI analyses demonstrated that the co‐primary endpoints were met, with GMRs for Ctrough(C3) and AUC0–84 of 1.39 (90% CI: 1.20–1.61) and 1.06 (90% CI: 0.92–1.21), respectively (Table S1). Additionally, slower SC absorption resulted in lower Cmax at the target mosunetuzumab SC dose of 45 mg as compared with the mosunetuzumab IV dose of 30 mg (median steady state Cmax was ~39% lower for simulated SC studies compared with simulated IV studies) (Figure 1).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: All patients in the mosunetuzumab SC cohort were evaluable for efficacy (N = 94); ORR and CR rate were 76.6% (95% CI: 66.7–84.7) and 61.7% (95% CI: 51.1–71.5), respectively. Median DOCR was 34.6 months (95% CI: 20.7–not evaluable [NE]), and median PFS was 23.7 months (95% CI: 14.6–NE) (Table 2; Figure 2). Median OS was not reached. The prespecified sensitivity analysis excluded one patient who died or discontinued treatment prior to having any tumor assessments due to COVID‐19, resulting in an ORR of 77.4% (95% CI: 67.6–85.5), CR rate of 62.4% (95% CI: 51.7–72.2), and a median PFS of 24.0 months (95% CI: 14.9–NE); median DOCR was unchanged (Table S2). Response rates, DOR, DOCR, and PFS with mosunetuzumab SC were similar to those observed with mosunetuzumab IV (Table 2; Figure 2).

sec.p: Within the mosunetuzumab SC cohort, clinically relevant CR rates were observed across all subgroups (Figure 3) and efficacy was maintained in patients with high‐risk disease features (Table S3). In patients with Ann Arbor stage III/IV disease, bulky disease (> 7 cm), and progression of disease within 24 months from start of first line therapy (POD24), CR rates were 61.0%, 59.1%, and 56.1%, respectively. CR rates were 50.0% and 42.9%, respectively, in patients who were double refractory to prior therapy and those with elevated lactate dehydrogenase. At 18 months, the PFS event‐free rate was 56.8% (95% CI: 46.4–67.2) in the overall population and ≥ 50% in all high‐risk subgroups (Table S3).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: The safety population included all 94 patients who received mosunetuzumab SC. AEs of any grade were reported in 98.9% of patients (Table 3). The most common AEs (reported in > 20% of patients) were injection site reactions (60.6%), fatigue (35.1%), CRS (29.8%), and diarrhea (20.2%) (Table S4). Grade 3/4 AEs were observed in 48.9% of patients and serious AEs in 39.4% of patients. Grade 5 (fatal) events (not including lymphoma progression) occurred in 5.3% of patients (COVID‐19 pneumonia [n = 2], and COVID‐19, general health deterioration, and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis [n = 1 each]). In addition to the five patients who died on treatment, two additional patients discontinued treatment due to COVID‐19 pneumonia and pneumonitis. AEs leading to mosunetuzumab SC dose interruption occurred in 40.4% of patients, most commonly COVID‐19 (12.8%) and neutropenia (10.6%). No AEs led to mosunetuzumab SC dose modification.

sec.p: The incidence of grade 3/4 AEs and serious AEs in the mosunetuzumab SC cohort was numerically lower than in the mosunetuzumab IV cohort. Rates of grade 5 AEs (5.3% vs. 1.1%) and AEs leading to discontinuation (7.4% vs. 4.4%) were low but numerically higher with mosunetuzumab SC than with IV (Table 3), reflective of the non‐concurrent enrollment and the impact of the COVID‐19 pandemic specifically on the SC cohort.

In the mosunetuzumab SC cohort, CRS events were reported in 29.8% of patients and were predominantly low grade (grade 1/2, 27.6%; grade 3, 2.1%) (Table S4). All events occurred during C1 (C1D1–7: 19.1%; C1D8–14: 12.8%; C1D15–21: 2.1%) (Figure 4). Serious AEs of CRS were reported in 16.0% of patients. Median (range) time to CRS onset from most recent mosunetuzumab dose was 2 (1–8) days and median (range) CRS duration was 2 (1–15) days. Eight patients (8.5%) received tocilizumab for the management of CRS, six (6.4%) received corticosteroids, and two (2.1%) received corticosteroids and tocilizumab (Table 3); all events had resolved by data cutoff.

sec.p: Infections were reported in 54.3% of patients in the mosunetuzumab SC cohort (grade 1/2, 35.1%; grade 3/4, 16.0%; grade 5, 3.2%) (Table S5; Table S6); infections not associated with COVID‐19 were reported in 39.4% of patients, most commonly upper respiratory tract infections (5.3%). Serious infections occurred in 17.0% of patients (Table S6). Overall, 66.0% of patients received antimicrobial prophylaxis; of these, 37.2% received trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and 45.7% received acyclovir/valacyclovir. Median time to onset of first infection and first serious infection was 64 days and 190 days, respectively; 91% of infections resolved.

COVID‐19 was reported in 19.1% of patients; most events were grade 1/2 (16.0%) (Table S4). Three COVID‐related AEs were grade 5 (COVID‐19 pneumonia [n = 2], COVID‐19 [n = 1]). No immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome events (preferred term) occurred. Neutropenia occurred in 21.3% of patients (grade 1/2, 3.2%; grade 3/4, 18.1%), and grade 3 febrile neutropenia concurrent with serious infection was reported in two patients. A total of 14 patients with neutropenia received treatment with granulocyte‐colony stimulating factor. Anemia occurred in 12.8% of patients (grade 1, 5.3%; grade 2, 1.1%; grade 3, 6.4%) and thrombocytopenia was reported in 11.7% of patients (grade 1, 4.3%; grade 2, 3.2%; grade 3, 3.2%; grade 4, 1.1%). All injection site reactions were grade 1 (53.2%) or 2 (7.4%) (Table S4). Injection site reactions (assessed using the high‐level term) occurred in 69.1% of patients and were grade 1 (59.6%) or grade 2 (9.6%). All but one patient had their events resolved by the clinical cutoff date, and no patients discontinued treatment due to injection‐site reactions. One patient had a grade 1 tumor flare event, and no events of tumor lysis syndrome were reported.

sec.title: Exploratory Pharmacodynamic Analysis
sec.p: Distinct cytokine release patterns were observed dependent on the route of mosunetuzumab administration. After initial C1D1 administration of mosunetuzumab IV, both IL‐6 and IFN‐γ levels increased; subsequent peaks were lower despite an increase in drug concentration. In comparison with mosunetuzumab IV, mosunetuzumab SC elicited a lower cytokine response (Figure S2). B‐cell depletion and recovery kinetics observed were similar between mosunetuzumab SC and mosunetuzumab IV (Figure S3A,B). Immunoglobulin (Ig) M kinetics followed the same pattern as B cell recovery and depletion, while IgG levels remained constant following mosunetuzumab administration (Figure S3C,D). IgM and IgG kinetics following mosunetuzumab SC administration were comparable to IV administration. Details on intratumoral CD20 expression can be found in the Supporting Information (Figure S4).

Overall completion rates for both patient‐reported measures were high (≥ 70%) while on treatment. The baseline mean (standard deviation [SD]) physical functioning and fatigue scores from the EORTC QLQ‐C30 questionnaire were 85.4 (20.3) and 25.8 (24.0), respectively, indicating normal physical functioning but slightly elevated fatigue levels. The baseline mean (SD) FACT‐Lym subscale score was 48.1 (9.6), indicating some burden of lymphoma‐specific symptoms. Following baseline, the mean scores for each domain were generally maintained while on treatment, indicating that mosunetuzumab SC treatment did not add additional burden to patients' HRQoL.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this pivotal Phase 2 study in heavily pretreated patients with R/R FL, mosunetuzumab SC met the co‐primary PK endpoints of the study, demonstrating non‐inferior exposure compared with mosunetuzumab IV. Similar efficacy, with high rates of complete and durable responses, was observed with mosunetuzumab SC (ORR: 76.6%; CR: 61.7%) compared with mosunetuzumab IV in the within‐study comparator cohort (ORR: 81.1%; CR: 60.0%). Clinically relevant efficacy was also observed with mosunetuzumab SC in patients with high‐risk disease features, including patients with POD24 and those who were double refractory to alkylator and anti‐CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy.

The safety profile of mosunetuzumab SC was manageable, with numerically lower rates and severity of CRS events compared with mosunetuzumab IV. CRS events were reported in 29.8% of patients in the mosunetuzumab SC cohort, compared with 44.4% of patients in the IV cohort; events were predominantly low grade and all occurred during C1. Grade 2 or higher CRS events occurred at a lower rate with mosunetuzumab SC compared with mosunetuzumab IV (9.6% vs. 18.9%). Serious AEs of CRS were reported in 16.0% of patients in the mosunetuzumab SC cohort and 23.3% in the mosunetuzumab IV cohort. Most CRS events were managed without the use of tocilizumab and/or corticosteroids and all events resolved. The majority of infections reported among patients in the mosunetuzumab SC cohort were low grade and events were manageable, with 91% of infections resolved. While a numerically higher rate of grade 5 AEs (5.3% vs. 1.1%) and AEs leading to treatment discontinuation (7.4% vs. 4.4%) were observed with mosunetuzumab SC versus IV, it should be noted that this was likely due to a greater impact of the COVID‐19 pandemic on the mosunetuzumab SC cohort in comparison with the IV cohort due to the non‐concurrent enrollment periods (SC enrollment: April 2021–February 2023; IV enrollment: May 2019–September 2020). Of the five grade 5 AEs reported with mosunetuzumab SC, three were due to COVID‐19, as were four of seven treatment discontinuations due to AEs. The impact of the COVID‐19 pandemic was also documented in studies of other CD20 × CD3 bispecific antibodies (epcoritamab and odronextamab) in R/R FL [4, 8].

In addition to the non‐inferior exposure of mosunetuzumab SC compared with mosunetuzumab IV, the slower absorption of mosunetuzumab SC resulted in lower Cmax at the SC target dose of 45 mg as compared to the IV dose of 30 mg, suggesting a mechanistic correlate with the lower CRS rates.

The mosunetuzumab IV cohort utilized copanlisib as a historical control for the primary efficacy endpoint of complete response [9]; however, copanlisib has since been withdrawn from the United States market by the FDA, along with the phosphatidylinositol 3‐kinase inhibitors umbralisib and duvelisib. The FL treatment landscape has undergone a shift since the design of the current study, with the approval of CAR T‐cell therapies and bispecific antibodies for the treatment of patients with R/R FL [24]. The response rates achieved with fixed‐duration mosunetuzumab SC were consistent with those observed with epcoritamab SC, a CD20 × CD3 bispecific antibody administered until disease progression, approved for the treatment of patients with R/R FL after ≥ 2 lines of therapy (ORR: 82.0%; CR: 62.5%) [4]. Notably, the incidence of CRS events (any grade) was considerably lower with mosunetuzumab SC (29.8%) compared with the pivotal epcoritamab cohort (66.4%), as well as a cohort of epcoritamab with an optimized step‐up dosing schedule (48.8%) [4]. An IV formulation of the CD20 × CD3 bispecific antibody odronextamab, administered until disease progression, has also obtained approval in the European Union for the treatment of patients with R/R FL after ≥ 2 lines of therapy [25]. In a Phase 2 study, ORR and CR rates with odronextamab were 80.0% and 73.4%, respectively [8]. For CRS mitigation, odronextamab IV is administered with a split‐dose step‐up dosing regimen, with inpatient monitoring during step‐up dosing and following the first full dose [8]. CRS events are common with odronextamab (any grade: 56.3%), occurring at a higher frequency than reported here with mosunetuzumab SC [8]. A SC formulation of odronextamab is currently being evaluated in the Phase 1 ELM‐1 study [26, 27]. The CAR T‐cell therapies lisocabtagene maraleucel, tisagenlecleucel, and axicabtagene ciloleucel, approved for the treatment of patients with R/R FL after ≥ 2 therapies, have demonstrated response rates of 97% (CR: 94%), 86.2% (CR: 69.1%), and 94% (CR: 79%), respectively, in this setting [5, 6, 7]. However, the use of CAR T‐cell therapies remains limited by logistical challenges, including the need for leukapheresis, lymphodepleting chemotherapy, specialized treatment centers, and centralized manufacturing processes [5, 28]. As an off‐the‐shelf treatment option, mosunetuzumab avoids these logistical challenges and can be administered without delay to patients requiring treatment. Another advantage of mosunetuzumab SC is the shorter administration time (30–60 s), while IV administration takes 2–4 h, facilitating outpatient treatment and thus potentially improving patient adherence, satisfaction, and overall healthcare utilization. The use of bispecific antibodies does not preclude later use of CAR T‐cell therapy due to the different target antigens (CD20 × CD3 vs. CD19), allowing both treatment classes to be used in sequence to optimize efficacy [29].

This is the first Phase 2 study with dose expansion cohorts for both an IV and SC formulation of the same bispecific antibody in lymphoma and includes a direct comparison of PK, CRS events, and efficacy. The use of a within‐study comparator cohort that enrolled at the same investigative sites is a strength of the study, and the mosunetuzumab SC and IV cohorts were well balanced in terms of sample size, baseline demographics, and disease characteristics. The non‐randomized design limits the interpretation of the study, although to date, data for other bispecific therapies in this setting are also derived from single‐arm studies [4, 8]. The greatest potential impact from the non‐concurrent enrollment of the two cohorts was the differing impact of the COVID‐19 pandemic, particularly with emergence of the COVID‐19 Omicron variant, which was more infectious than previous strains, during enrollment of the SC cohort. This is reflected in the higher rates of COVID‐19 infections and grade 5 events with mosunetuzumab SC in comparison with mosunetuzumab IV. However, sensitivity analyses adjusting for COVID‐19 mortality (excluding one patient) showed similar response rates with mosunetuzumab SC, and B‐cell depletion and recovery and immunoglobulin kinetics were comparable with the IV formulation.

In conclusion, factors related to quality of life are of utmost importance to patients with FL, and SC formulations have become a preferred mode of administration [30, 31]. The primary objectives of the study were met, with safety and efficacy results supporting the positive benefit–risk profile of the mosunetuzumab SC formulation. Data from the subgroup analyses were encouraging but limited by small sample sizes.

Mosunetuzumab SC provides practical and clinical advantages over IV administration, offering the potential for comparable efficacy with notable improvements in safety and tolerability, combined with the convenience of an off‐the‐shelf, fixed‐duration treatment with a lower administration burden. Reduced healthcare resource utilization is anticipated compared with IV dosing. Further studies exploring the use of mosunetuzumab SC in earlier lines of therapy and other lymphoma subtypes are warranted.

sec.title: Ethics Statement
sec.p: This study was conducted in full conformance with the International Council for Harmonisation E6 guideline for Good Clinical Practice and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, or the applicable laws and regulations of the country in which the research was conducted, whichever afforded greater protection to the individual. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: Qualified researchers may request access to individual patient‐level data through the clinical study data request platform (https://vivli.org/). Further details on Roche's criteria for eligible studies are available at https://vivli.org/members/ourmembers/. For further details on Roche's Global Policy on the Sharing of Clinical Information and how to request access to related clinical study documents, see https://www.roche.com/research_and_development/who_we_are_how_we_work/clinical_trials/our_commitment_to_data_sharing.htm.
